summary: When a BGP peer or a link fails, alternate paths should be used quickly. This informational RFC gives a basic methodology for benchmarking BGP data-plane convergence, so that vendors and operators can measure and compare how fast a router switches traffic to backup paths.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road closes, how fast do drivers find a new route? This gives a fair way to time it so different routers can be compared.

questions: how to measure bgp data plane convergence
how to measure route failover time
subtitle: How to measure how fast routers switch to backup paths when a link fails

tldr.problem: Internet routing depends on BGP to switch traffic to alternate paths when links fail. Service providers want to know: how fast does a router converge? But without a standard way to measure, vendors report different numbers and comparisons are meaningless.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a standardized methodology for benchmarking BGP data-plane convergence. It specifies test topologies with three or four nodes, documented procedures for triggering failures and measuring timing, parameter settings, and how to report results so that different routers can be compared fairly.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can now measure and compare how quickly routers update their forwarding tables after BGP route changes or failures, enabling informed purchasing decisions and network design choices.

today: RFC 7747 is an Informational RFC published in April 2016 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary methodology for benchmarking BGP data-plane convergence and is widely referenced by vendors, operators, and testing labs as the standard for comparing router convergence performance.

sections.title: BGP Convergence and Data-Plane Performance
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the routing protocol of the Internet. When a link fails or a BGP peer goes down, BGP must find an alternate path. The routing information base (RIB) receives updates, and the forwarding information base (FIB) is recalculated and updated to switch traffic to the new route.

Convergence time is how long this takes. Service providers care about convergence time because even a few seconds of packet loss can affect critical applications. Network operators want to minimize convergence time and ensure their routers are fast.

However, vendors reported convergence times in different ways, making it impossible to compare a Cisco router to a Juniper router, or to compare older versions to newer ones. This RFC solves that problem by defining a standard methodology.

The focus is on data-plane convergence (how fast the FIB updates), not control-plane convergence (how fast the RIB updates). It applies to both IPv4 and IPv6, and covers both eBGP (external, between autonomous systems) and iBGP (internal, within an autonomous system).
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is the system that tells routers how to send traffic across the Internet. When a route breaks, it takes time to find a new one. This explains how to measure that time fairly so routers can be compared.

sections.title: Test Topologies and Setup
sections.content:
The RFC defines four standard test topologies, each with three to four nodes:

Basic test setup: A Device Under Test (DUT) has two routing interfaces connected to an emulator that simulates multiple BGP peers and generates traffic. This is used for basic convergence tests.

Three-node setup: A Helper Node runs the same BGP version as the DUT. The DUT is connected to both the Helper Node and an emulator. This setup measures RIB-OUT convergence (how fast the DUT forwards new routes to its neighbors).

eBGP Multihop setup: Similar to three-node but includes loopback interfaces. It measures multihop eBGP convergence where the BGP session is not directly between adjacent routers.

Four-node setup: A more complex topology with two Helper Nodes connected in series with the DUT. It can measure convergence in iBGP or eBGP scenarios with more intermediate nodes.

All devices must be synchronized using NTP to ensure timestamps are accurate. Traffic flows in and out of the DUT, and convergence is measured by watching when traffic successfully traverses the DUT after a route change.
sections.plainLanguage: The test uses a simple network with a router being tested (DUT) and other devices that pretend to be neighbors. When a route breaks, the test measures how long until traffic flows again.

sections.title: Convergence Test Cases
sections.content:
The RFC defines multiple test cases to measure different aspects of convergence:

RIB-IN Convergence: Measures how fast a route received from a neighbor is installed in the routing information base. A neighbor advertises a route, and the test records when the DUT sends data traffic over that route.

RIB-OUT Convergence: Measures how fast the DUT receives a route, installs it, and advertises it to another neighbor. This involves three devices: emulator (source), DUT (middle), and Helper Node (destination).

eBGP and iBGP Convergence: Similar to RIB-OUT but specifically for external BGP (between autonomous systems) or internal BGP (within an autonomous system).

eBGP Multihop Convergence: Tests convergence when BGP peers are not directly connected but several hops apart.

Failure-triggered convergence: Instead of advertising a new route, the test simulates a physical link failure, BGP adjacency failure, or other error condition on the DUT, and measures how long until traffic reroutes.

Route withdrawal: Measures convergence when a route is withdrawn (deleted), forcing traffic to use an alternate path.

Path attribute changes and graceful restart: Test how convergence is affected when route attributes change or when BGP graceful restart mechanisms are used.

For each test, the procedure specifies exactly what to do: establish peers, start traffic, advertise routes, record timestamps, and calculate convergence time as the difference between when a route is received and when data traffic is observed on the egress interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Different tests measure different things: how fast a route is learned, how fast it is shared with neighbors, and how fast traffic switches when a route breaks. Each test has exact steps so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: Configuration and Measurement Parameters
sections.content:
Many parameters affect BGP convergence time. To enable fair comparison, the RFC specifies which parameters to use in baseline tests:

BGP timers: Keepalive interval (default 1 minute), holdtime (default 3 minutes), update delay timer (default 0 seconds), ConnectRetry timer (default 1 second), and MinASOriginationInterval (default 0).

TCP parameters: Segment size (default 4096 bytes), maximum window size, MTU (maximum transmission unit), and authentication method (TCP AO or TCP MD5).

Route advertisement parameters: Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI, default 0 seconds) controls how fast consecutive route updates are sent.

Link failure detection: Interface failure detection timer (default 0 ms for immediate detection).

Policy settings: Route filtering policies should be set to a minimal policy for baseline tests.

For baseline tests, most of these should be set to defaults or zero. However, operators might also run tests with their real-world parameters to see how convergence is affected. All settings must be documented in the test report.

Tests should be repeated multiple times with different route mixtures and numbers of routes. Results should report average, mean, and standard deviation to account for variability.
sections.plainLanguage: Many things can slow down convergence: waiting for timer to expire, authentication processing, route filtering. The test says which settings to use so that different routers are tested fairly.

sections.title: Measurement Accuracy and Reporting
sections.content:
Convergence is measured using packet loss as the timing signal. When data traffic targeted at a route stops arriving at the egress interface, that is when the FIB has not yet been updated. When traffic starts arriving again, the FIB has been updated and convergence is complete. The convergence time is the gap between when the route change occurred and when traffic arrives.

Accuracy depends on the packet transmission interval. If packets are sent every 100 milliseconds, convergence can be measured with a resolution of 100 ms. For better accuracy, the RFC mentions alternative methods: Time-Based Loss Method (TBLM) and Timestamp-Based Method (TBM) defined in RFC 6414.

Devices must have synchronized time (using NTP) and measurement instruments must capture the exact moment of route advertisement and the moment traffic is received.

Results should be reported in a standard format documenting:

  • Test setup (topology, number of peers, number of routes per peer)
  • Configuration parameters (all timer values, policies, authentication)
  • Route mixture and advertisement rate
  • For each test run: the route that triggered convergence, the convergence time in milliseconds, and packet loss during convergence
  • Statistical summary: average, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum convergence times across multiple runs
sections.plainLanguage: The test watches when traffic stops arriving and when it starts again after a route change. The time between those two events is the convergence time. Tests should be done several times and results should show the average and how much they vary.

sections.title: Status and Use
sections.content:
RFC 7747 is an Informational RFC published in April 2016 and has not been obsoleted. It has become the industry standard for benchmarking BGP convergence and is widely used by vendors and service providers.

The RFC defines methodology for basic convergence tests using simple topologies. More complex scenarios (IGP interaction, VPN convergence, segment routing) are not covered and may be defined in future documents.

The methodology enables standardized, repeatable measurements that can be compared across different router platforms and software versions, allowing operators to make informed decisions about network equipment and network design.
sections.plainLanguage: This document set the standard that everybody uses now. It makes it possible to fairly compare how fast different routers are at switching to backup paths.
